name: Manlet / height tiers

lead: Manlet is forum slang for a man regarded as short, and height tiers are the informal brackets members use to rank men by height. The vocabulary frames why so many people in appearance communities work on height, lifts, posture and presentation.

There is no single mechanism; it is a way of classifying height and discussing how it shapes perceived status. Posters disagree about where the cutoffs sit. Medicine defines short stature as adult height more than two standard deviations below the mean for age and sex, roughly the shortest 2.3 percent of a population, which is separate from the community's brackets.

paras: People use the terms in advice threads, comparison photos and memes, then turn to practical options discussed alongside them such as lifts, posture, fit and clothing, and growth-focused routines for those still growing.

The term is used as a pejorative as well as a self-description. Medical sources describe teasing reported by short children, and one Swedish cohort study reported an inverse association between height and suicide risk in men, while noting most very short adults are not disabled by their height.

angle.text: Manlet and height tiers are the shorthand for how height is ranked in appearance communities, and they explain why users chase height gains, lifts and sharper presentation. It is a vocabulary rather than a method, and cutoffs vary by poster.

lead: Manlet is slang used on looksmaxxing forums such as looksmax.org for a man considered short, often paired with the idea of height tiers: informal brackets of height used to rank men within the community. Posters disagree about where the thresholds sit, and threads exist both asserting and disputing particular cutoffs. The vocabulary matters for appearance because height is treated as one of the most visible and least changeable parts of how a man looks, and it frames the community's interest in options that add height or change how tall a man appears, from footwear to surgery. [1][2][3][4]

Medically, short stature is usually defined as adult height more than two standard deviations below the mean for age and sex, about the shortest 2.3 percent of a population, and common childhood causes include constitutional growth delay and familial short stature. The community vocabulary is separate from this definition. Height has also been studied by economists and psychologists, who report associations between height and earnings, partner preference and, in one large Swedish cohort, suicide risk [5].

Height features heavily in forum discussion, where members post about perceived social disadvantage, rage threads, and heightmaxxing options such as growth hormone secretagogues [1][2]. Outside looksmaxxing, the same word is used humorously: strength-sport forums such as T Nation use manlet as light-hearted self-description or banter [6][7][8].

The word itself is recent. Wiktionary defines it as a short man and labels the seduction-community sense derogatory; its earliest dated citation is from 2015 and a 2022 media piece titled What's a 'Manlet'? is also listed, though the entry gives no first known use [9].

paras: Manlet is applied to men judged short, usually by the poster. Titles on looksmax.org use it for videos, fights, celebrity comparisons and personal threads, for example 'Manlet rage' and 'manlet problems' [1][2]. Height tiers refers to ranking by height bracket in the same culture, with the brackets decided by users rather than any authority.

The term is associated with the broader hierarchy vocabulary of the forum, including mogging, where a taller or more attractive person is said to outclass another. Thread titles pair manlets with 'heightmogging' by taller people on the news, with celebrity comparisons involving actors such as Will Poulter and Daniel Radcliffe, and with the opposite storyline of a short man winning a fight against a taller opponent or attracting a partner [10][11][12][13].

A related piece of vocabulary is the heightpill: the belief, expressed in thread titles such as one about a manlet raging against it, that height is a fixed and decisive factor in how men are treated [14]. Where height tiers are laid out, users typically define a handful of brackets from very short to very tall; the numbers differ between posters and are not drawn from a published standard.

sections.h: Average height and tiers in context
paras: Mean adult male height varies across populations and over time. Young Dutch men averaged about 183 cm by 2012, compared with about 164 cm in 1829, and average heights in industrialised countries rose by up to 10 cm in the 150 years after the mid-1800s before levelling off. Twin studies put height at roughly 60 to 80 percent heritable, and a 2014 study of 253,288 people identified 697 variants at 423 loci. Because tiers in forums are fixed numbers while population averages differ, the same absolute height can be placed in different brackets depending on the community's reference population.

Wikipedia's article on human height lists other benchmarks: England in the first half of the 1700s averaged about 165 cm for men, ancient Rome about 169 cm, and young South Korean men in the mid-1990s cohort were about 12 cm taller than their North Korean counterparts after decades of different nutrition. Nutrition, especially protein, illness in childhood and socioeconomic conditions all affect final height, and growth is fastest in infancy and puberty.

sections.h: History of height as a social marker
paras: Sociologist Saul Feldman coined the term heightism in 1971 in a paper presented to the American Sociological Association, and the word entered the Second Barnhart Dictionary of New English the same year. Wikipedia's article describes height-based discrimination in hiring and promotion and notes cases such as a 2005 Swedish Labour Court ruling on a Volvo height requirement and a 2022 Spanish Supreme Court decision on police height rules.

Militaries have long used height limits. In the First World War, Britain's minimum soldier height was 5 ft 3 in (160 cm), and shorter men served in about 29 Bantam Battalions of roughly 1,000 men each. Some jobs still set height ranges, such as US Air Force pilots, who must be between 160 and 200 cm.

Several jurisdictions prohibit height discrimination. Michigan has done so since the 1976 Elliott-Larsen Civil Rights Act, New York City's law covering height and weight was signed on 26 May 2023, and Ontario and Victoria (Australia) also prohibit it.

Forum members discuss several routes to being or looking taller. Shoe lifts, also called elevator shoes, are thickened sections inside the heel that raise the wearer while remaining hidden from observers, unlike visible high heels [3]. Posture and footwear changes add apparent height without altering the skeleton.

Growth hormone injections are prescribed for children with diagnosed growth failure for several years and typically add about 5 to 10 cm to final adult height, at costs Wikipedia puts around US$20,000 a year for a small child and above US$50,000 for a teenager. Forum threads also discuss growth hormone secretagogues such as MK-677 for teenagers, an off-label use; one poster aged 17 asks whether it is worthwhile [2]. No published study has tested MK-677 for height in healthy short people.

Cosmetic limb lengthening uses surgical techniques developed from the Ilizarov method, in which a bone is cut and gradually separated at about 1 mm per day, or from motorized implanted nails such as the Fitbone [4]. Wikipedia reports that demand is high in India, where press reports from 2016 described patients as young as 13 or 14, infections that needed further surgery and gains smaller than expected, and that China's Ministry of Health banned the procedure in 2006 after a series of operations caused serious side effects [4]. Reported complication rates in the limb-lengthening literature include infection in about 5 percent, bone growing in the wrong direction in 7 to 9 percent and hardware failure in 3 to 4.5 percent [4]. The wiki does not give procedural instructions.

In one thread, a teenage poster aged 17 who describes himself as 5'5 asks whether MK-677 would be worthwhile for height, citing side effects he has heard of such as grogginess, hunger, water retention and diabetes risk. Replies in the thread include advice to accept one's height and be confident, as well as rejection of that advice [2].

Another thread describes the poster as short and expresses distress about being so, drawing a reply in the same terms [1]. Other threads present video clips of short men said to be outclassed, or mogged, by taller people [15]. Posters who identify as manlets also post fight clips and celebrity comparisons as evidence for or against the importance of height [12][13].

sections.h: Use in strength and fitness communities
paras: On T Nation the word recurs in training logs. Members call themselves manlets while discussing lifting, one writing that being shorter lets them 'grow sideways', another joking that tall people only have an advantage in reaching high shelves and in running [6][7]. A powerlifter notes that lifting slippers were hard to find in small sizes labelled for manlets [16]. A 6'2 member describes himself as a giant among manlets on the forum [17]. In these threads the label is used humorously rather than as a rank.

Short children often report being teased, though the encyclopedic summary notes that most very short adults are not physically or psychologically disabled by their height. A Swedish cohort study of about 1.3 million men found each 5 cm of height was linked to roughly a 9 percent lower suicide risk, while later studies found the effect of height on quality of life to be small and tied more to dissatisfaction with one's height than to height itself. A 2025 narrative review in PLOS Mental Health by Schmidt and Talbot examined height dissatisfaction and its links to self-esteem, body image concern, anxiety and depression, and noted that research is limited, especially on clinical populations [5].

Economists report a height premium in wages: Persico and colleagues found about 1.8 percent higher wages per inch in a 2004 study, and Judge and Cable (2004) found height strongly tied to income and workplace success among men, even after controlling for age and weight. Surveys cited in the same source report that fewer than 3 percent of CEOs in one 1995 count were under 1.70 m. Taller US presidential candidates won 22 of 25 elections in the twentieth century, though sex and socioeconomic status may explain part of the link between height and success.

On dating, studies cited by Wikipedia report that American women in one study by Dan Ariely preferred taller men, with a 5'4 man needing substantially more income than a 6'0 man to be equally appealing; a 2009 study of Hadza foragers found height did not matter in their mate choice, which the authors took to suggest the preference varies by culture. A 2022 cross-cultural study in Frontiers in Psychology of over 500 people from Canada, Cuba, Norway and the United States found that participants on average preferred taller-than-average male partners and shorter-than-average female partners, with the preference present across samples [5].

The idea of a Napoleon complex, a purported link between short men and aggression, is described by psychologists mostly as a stereotype. Napoleon himself is estimated at about 1.67 m, roughly average for his era. Some studies support the notion, such as a Groningen finding that 1.63 m men were more likely to show jealousy than 1.98 m men, and a 2022 paper linking antagonistic traits to dissatisfaction with height; others, such as a 2007 University of Central Lancashire experiment and the Wessex Growth Study, found no personality differences attributable to height.

Growth hormone therapy for children with growth failure typically adds about 5 to 10 cm to predicted final height over years of injections, and critics have argued drug makers promoted short stature as a disease; Wikipedia reports a proposed screening scheme estimated to add 90,000 customers and US$10 billion in revenue, and that about half of treated children did not have growth hormone deficiency. Height discrimination is illegal in some places: Michigan prohibits it in the United States, as do Ontario and Victoria, and in 2022 Spain's Supreme Court ruled that police height requirements must reflect average height for each sex.

Height has health correlations too. Wikipedia reports that shorter people tend to have lower blood pressure and less cancer, that several human studies estimate a loss of about 0.5 years of life per added cm of height, and that very tall people can have heart and mobility problems.

No studies found on the community term or the height tiers themselves. Related research on short stature and growth hormone therapy in children is summarised in encyclopedic sources, and research on height and social outcomes is summarised under Research and expert views.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, manlet threads mix humour, self-deprecation and questions about height-increasing methods [1][2]. On T Nation the same word is mostly playful [6][7].

claims.claim: Being short is a major, hard-to-change disadvantage (the 'heightpill').
Drugs like MK-677 can add height for a teenager who is short.
Confidence and presentation can offset height.
Short men are more aggressive (the 'Napoleon complex').
Women strongly prefer taller men, so height tiers predict dating success.
Limb lengthening surgery is a route to a taller frame.

timeline.event: Alessandro Codivilla publishes the first clinical attempt at limb lengthening, in 26 people with malformed legs [4].
Gavriil Ilizarov begins decades of work on gradual bone lengthening, later the basis of external-fixator limb lengthening [4].
Sociologist Saul Feldman coins the term heightism for prejudice based on height.
Michigan's Elliott-Larsen Civil Rights Act prohibits height discrimination.
The BBC comedy A Small Problem depicts discrimination against people under five feet.
Studies by Judge and Cable and by Persico and colleagues report a height premium in wages.
A Swedish cohort study of about 1.3 million men reports an inverse link between height and suicide risk.
China's Ministry of Health bans cosmetic limb lengthening after operations caused serious side effects [4].
Earliest dated citation of manlet recorded by Wiktionary [9].
Spain's Supreme Court rules that police height requirements must reflect average height for each sex; a cross-cultural study reports preferences for taller male partners [5].
New York City signs a law prohibiting height and weight discrimination (26 May).
A narrative review of height dissatisfaction and psychological outcomes is published in PLOS Mental Health [5].
